p00.title: Try this in a terminal
p00.intro: A practice run of the Git workflow every later phase uses: start a repository, work on a branch, and merge it back, including a merge conflict on purpose. Run it in a new folder so nothing else is affected. On Windows, use Git Bash or PowerShell 7; Windows PowerShell 5 does not understand && (run the two commands on separate lines).

lines.0: Make an empty folder for the practice and move into it.
lines.1: Turn the folder into a Git repository. Git creates a hidden .git folder that stores every version.
lines.2: Create two files with any text in them, so there is something to save.
lines.3: Stage every file (add) and save a snapshot (commit) with a message saying what it is.
lines.4: Create a branch called feature/calculator and switch to it. Work here does not touch main.
lines.5: Change app.py, then git add app.py and git commit -m "..." to save the change on this branch.
lines.6: Go back to the main branch. app.py returns to how it was before the branch.
lines.7: Edit the same line of app.py differently and commit it, so the two branches disagree.
lines.8: Bring the branch into main. Git stops with a conflict: open app.py, keep the right lines, delete the <<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>> markers, then git add app.py and git commit.

p00.after: You are done when git log --oneline --graph shows both branches joining in a merge commit. A merge conflict is normal: it means two changes touched the same lines and Git needs you to choose.

p02.title: What this phase's code looks like
p02.intro: Not a command to run: a picture of what you will be able to write by the end of the phase. Each piece is a Python feature this phase teaches you to build yourself.

lines.0: A decorator you write: it wraps fetch and measures how long each call takes.
lines.1: A decorator that takes arguments: retry the call up to 3 times, waiting longer (2x) after each failure.
lines.2: A function with type hints: url is a str and the function returns bytes.
lines.3: The body is left out here. ... is valid Python that means 'nothing yet'.
lines.5: A context manager you write: set something up, hand it over as r, and always clean it up, even after an error.
lines.6: The code that uses r goes here. When the block ends, cleanup runs automatically.

p02.after: By the end you can write @timer, @retry and managed_resource from a blank file and explain what Python does with each.

p03.title: The commands a finished package passes
p03.intro: What a real Python project runs before every release. Your goal in this phase is a project where all six succeed. Run them from the project's folder, the one with pyproject.toml.

lines.0: Create a virtual environment (.venv, a private copy of Python for this project) and switch to it. On Windows use .venv\Scripts\activate instead of source .venv/bin/activate.
lines.1: Install your project in editable mode (-e: code changes apply without reinstalling), plus its [dev] tools listed in pyproject.toml.
lines.2: Lint (ruff check finds bugs and bad patterns) and check formatting without changing files.
lines.3: Type-check the code in src/ with mypy: it finds wrong types before the code runs.
lines.4: Run the tests quietly (-q). Every one should pass.
lines.5: Run your installed command. If --help prints usage, the package installed correctly.

p03.after: You are done when all six run without an error on a fresh clone of your repository. The same commands then go into CI so they run on every push.

p04.title: The layout you will build
p04.intro: Not a command: the folder structure of this phase's project, pystructures. You implement each data structure yourself, test it and measure it.

lines.1: A dynamic array (like Python's list) and a linked list.
lines.2: A stack (last in, first out) and a queue (first in, first out).
lines.3: A hash table (like dict) and a binary search tree.
lines.4: A heap (priority queue), a graph with searches, and a trie (prefix tree).
lines.5: Timing scripts that compare your structures with Python's built-ins, and the tests for every file.

p04.after: Each file has tests, and benchmarks/ shows where your version is slower than the built-in and why.

p15.title: The system you will build
p15.intro: Not a command: a diagram of this phase's project. Requests come into an API and are queued; several workers process them; failures are kept and can be replayed; everything is observable.

lines.0: The API takes requests and puts jobs on the queue instead of doing slow work itself.
lines.2: The queue holds jobs. A job that keeps failing moves to a dead-letter queue, where you can inspect it and replay it once fixed.
lines.4: Several workers take jobs from the queue in parallel. Add workers to handle more load.
lines.6: Workers write results to the database, the one source of truth.
lines.8: A cache in front of the database answers repeated reads quickly.
lines.10: Traces, metrics and logs show what every part is doing, so you can find a slow or failing step.

p15.after: You are done when you can kill a worker, stop the database for a minute, or flood the queue, and the system recovers without losing a job.
